source.title: Compute Optimal Scaling of Skills: Knowledge vs Reasoning
source.authors: Nicholas Roberts; Niladri S. Chatterji; Sharan Narang; Mike Lewis; Dieuwke Hupkes

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures skill-specific compute optima and shows that they vary with skill, pretraining data mix, and validation-set composition. These results qualify how generally a compute-optimal allocation can be applied; it also reports that a 2D power-law model fit poorly to its downstream evaluations.
record.gate_note: The paper trains models across compute scales and measures target-answer NLL on knowledge-QA and code datasets, then estimates skill-specific compute optima. It also reports validation-set NLLs and changes in estimated optima. Cited results from Kaplan et al., Hoffmann et al., and Dubey et al. are not recorded as this study’s results. It does not test generic held-out pretraining loss or small-run extrapolation.
record.test_reason: The study trains IsoFLOP sweeps from 6e18 to 3e21 FLOPs (40M–8B parameters). It shows that the loss-minimising parameter/token split depends on the target loss (knowledge-QA vs code NLL vs the Llama-3 APE fit), on the pretraining datamix, and on the validation set. These are direct results on how general a single compute-optimal allocation is (V3) and on setup-dependence of the optimum (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude that the datamix can be tuned so that knowledge and code optima align (code about 2.1× knowledge), though no validation set tracked both skills. Knowledge's capacity-hunger grows faster with skill data, which they attribute to knowledge being harder to compress. Validation-set mismatch shifts the optimal parameter count by over 30% at the smallest scale and over 10% at the largest three.
record.recipe_differences: Uses IsoFLOP sweeps and NLL-based optima, with a Dubey et al. (2024)-style recipe; differs from a direct reproduction of the original studies by focusing on downstream skill datasets, fitting per-compute quadratic curves, and comparing their optima across skills and data mixtures.
record.method_sensitivity: Skill type, proportion of skill-relevant pretraining data, validation-set composition, and loss-fitting approach change the reported optima or fit quality.
record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (2025)
record.problems: The datamix ablations and part of the validation-set analysis use only the smallest compute scale, 6 × 10^18 FLOPs. The authors note limited hypothesis and held-out benchmark sizes, noise in knowledge-QA results, and an inability to validate their non-Python-language observation rigorously. No uncertainty estimates are stated in the provided text.
record.rows_left_out: Individual benchmark IsoFLOP and datamix curves are shown in Figures 11–18 but are not transcribed as separate numerical rows; the paper’s explicit aggregate and all-dataset directional statements are recorded in r1–r5. The plotted curves do not provide tabulated uncertainty estimates.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a power law in N, D or C is not reported. The APE fit is taken from Dubey et al.
The fitted exponents for skill optima are not reported numerically. The study does not compare Kaplan and Hoffmann prescriptions, and does not check token-count growth separately.
Shape is not varied at fixed parameter count.
Downstream target NLL is measured across scales, but its predictability from scale or loss is not tested or quantified.
Parameter counting, training schedule, and fitting method (beyond the anecdotal r11) are not tested.

missing.what: Fig 1c distribution of log parameter-count residuals: knowledge and code means lie on opposite sides of the APE CO across 9 compute scales
The CO alignment crossover ratio of code to knowledge is 2.1 on the hypothesis split and 2.7 on the held-out split
Validation-set IsoFLOP optima across all compute scales: FineWeb and FineWeb-Edu are capacity-hungry relative to The Stack
Multi-language code benchmarks are more capacity-hungry than Python-only ones (not validated on the held-out split)

record.verdict_notes: The APE baseline is the Dubey et al. (2024) fitted law projected onto this study's curves, not an optimum the study measured itself. The datamix ablations (r3–r6) use only 6e18 FLOPs, so they bear on V7 but not on how the optimum scales with compute. No uncertainty estimates are given.

versions.untested_parts: The paper measures downstream skill NLL, not held-out pretraining loss as a power law in parameter count, tokens, or compute.
It does not test predictions from small runs against runs orders of magnitude larger.

It studies skill-specific compute optima across compute scales, but does not establish that both parameter count and token count follow stable powers of compute or compare the reported growth rates with the Kaplan and Hoffmann prescriptions.
It varies model dimensions to construct different model sizes but does not compare architectures at fixed parameter count.
It studies text pretraining and skill datasets only; it does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Although downstream skill NLL is measured across scales, the study does not test whether downstream performance is predictably forecast from scale or pretraining loss.
The study tests sensitivity to skill, data mix, validation set, and its chosen loss-fitting approach, but not parameter-counting conventions or alternative training schedules.

rows.subject: models (held-out knowledge-QA dataset average)
rows.operation_detail: Compared skill-specific IsoFLOP optima with APE optima across compute scales using target-answer NLL.
rows.measure: Skill compute-optimal parameter count relative to the APE compute optimum
rows.baseline: APE CO from Dubey et al. (2024)
rows.value: Knowledge QA is capacity-hungry relative to the APE CO, especially at lower compute scales.
rows.note: The reported result concerns parameter-count residuals and relative allocation, not an explicit test of stable power-law growth in both parameters and tokens.
rows.check: The state should be observed: every knowledge dataset in both splits is capacity-hungry (Figs 11–12, Fig 1c). The baseline is not this study's own validation loss; it is the Dubey et al. power-law APE CO projected onto the curves. The record's 'partial' conflates the effect with untested parts of V3.

rows.subject: models (held-out code dataset average)
rows.operation_detail: Compared skill-specific IsoFLOP optima with APE optima across compute scales using target-answer NLL.
rows.measure: Skill compute-optimal parameter count relative to the APE compute optimum
rows.baseline: APE CO from Dubey et al. (2024)
rows.value: Code tends to be data-hungry relative to the APE CO.
rows.note: The study reports the average pattern and says it also holds across individual datasets.
rows.check: The state should be observed: every code dataset in both splits is data-hungry (Figs 13–14). SWE-bench was excluded from the averages because its optima fell outside the model range. The baseline is the Dubey et al. APE fit (a cited result).

rows.subject: models (held-out code dataset average)
rows.operation_detail: Varied the proportion of code in the pretraining data and recomputed code skill IsoFLOP curves and optima.
rows.measure: Target NLL and skill compute-optimal parameter count
rows.value: As code data increased, held-out code losses improved and COs shifted toward capacity-hunger.
rows.note: The paper describes these as average held-out code results; the strongest pattern is reported for code.
rows.check: Single compute scale (6e18), so it cannot speak to how the optimum grows with compute (V3). Link to V7 only. The top code share is 82.02% (the text also says 84%).

rows.subject: models (held-out knowledge-QA dataset average)
rows.operation_detail: Varied the proportion of knowledge data in the pretraining data and recomputed knowledge-QA skill IsoFLOP curves and optima.
rows.measure: Target NLL and skill compute-optimal parameter count
rows.value: Increasing knowledge data improved losses and shifted knowledge-QA COs toward capacity-hunger; the authors note that these results are noisier than the code results.
rows.note: The paper reports the average held-out trend and cautions that knowledge results are noisier.
rows.check: Single compute scale, so it bears on V7 only. Partial is right: the knowledge results are noisier, and held-out MMLU does not follow the pattern (Fig 16).

rows.subject: models (knowledge-QA and code dataset averages)
rows.operation_detail: Compared optimal parameter count as a function of the proportion of skill-relevant data for knowledge QA and code.
rows.measure: Optimal parameter count at a given proportion of skill-relevant data
rows.baseline: Comparison between knowledge-QA and code optima at the same skill-relevant-data proportion
rows.value: Knowledge QA requires more parameters on average and its optimal parameter count increases more quickly as the relevant-data proportion rises.
rows.note: The authors interpret the difference as persisting after accounting for skill-relevant-data proportions.
rows.check: Single compute scale; V7 only. No numbers given beyond the figure (roughly 250–400M parameters).

rows.subject: models (same skill, different datamixes)
rows.operation_detail: Compared estimated optimal parameter counts across datamixes.
rows.measure: Variation in estimated optimal parameter count
rows.baseline: Other datamixes for the same skill
rows.value: The optimal parameter count for the same skill varies by 30% or more across datamixes; the introduction reports almost 50% across datamixes on the smallest-scale experiments.
rows.note: The paper reports sensitivity of the estimated optimum to data composition.
rows.check: Subject is wrong. Per the conclusion and Fig 6a–b, this is the validation-set APE optimum across code/knowledge ratios, not a skill optimum. The numbers are mixed up: the conclusion gives ≥30% across datamixes for a single validation set and almost 50% depending on the validation set, while the intro gives 'almost 50% across datamixes'. Single compute scale.

rows.subject: models (FineWeb validation set)
rows.operation_detail: Measured validation NLL and estimated APE optima using a sampled validation set.
rows.measure: Validation NLL as code data increases
rows.value: FineWeb loss monotonically increases with the amount of code data; validation-set COs can differ from The Stack by up to roughly 50% across the examined settings.
rows.note: The NLL trend is stated explicitly; the maximum relative CO difference is reported across validation sets and settings.
rows.check: Merges two results: the NLL trend versus code ratio (Fig 5b) and the optimum difference from The Stack of up to about 50% (Fig 6b). Only the latter bears directly on the optimum.

rows.subject: models (FineWeb-Edu validation set)
rows.operation_detail: Measured validation NLL and estimated APE optima using a sampled validation set.
rows.measure: Validation NLL as code data increases
rows.value: FineWeb-Edu loss monotonically increases with the amount of code data; its estimated optima differ from The Stack depending on the setting.
rows.note: The authors say FineWeb and FineWeb-Edu track knowledge QA more closely than code.
rows.check: Same merge as r7. Fig 10/App. H shows FineWeb-Edu is capacity-hungry relative to The Stack at all compute scales.

rows.subject: models (The Stack validation set)
rows.operation_detail: Measured validation NLL and estimated APE optima using a sampled validation set.
rows.measure: Validation NLL as code data increases; reference CO for validation-set comparison
rows.baseline: Other code-to-knowledge ratios; reference for relative CO differences
rows.value: The Stack loss moves in the opposite direction to FineWeb and FineWeb-Edu as code data increases; used as the baseline for reported relative parameter-count differences.
rows.note: The text identifies The Stack as code-aligned and uses it as the relative-CO baseline.
rows.check: The Stack is the reference baseline for the relative optimum differences, not a result in itself. Its NLL trend only shows which skill it tracks. This is better folded into r7/r8/r10 than kept as a separate row.

rows.subject: models (aggregate validation-set comparison)
rows.operation_detail: Compared estimated optimal parameter counts across validation sets and compute scales.

conditions.value: smallest scale 6 × 10^18 FLOPs; largest three scales up to 3 × 10^21 FLOPs

rows.measure: Relative difference in optimal parameter count
rows.value: At the smallest compute scale, different validation sets produce over 30% difference in optimal parameter count; the difference exceeds 10% for the three largest compute scales.
rows.note: The abstract and conclusion also describe nearly 50% variation depending on validation-set composition.
rows.check: Bears on V3: the estimated optimum across compute scales shifts by more than 10% even at the three largest scales (up to 3e21), depending on the validation set.

rows.subject: models (downstream skill evaluations)
rows.operation_detail: Compared a 2D power-law loss model with fitting separate degree-2 polynomials at each compute scale.

conditions.value: 2D power-law model versus per-compute-scale degree-2 polynomials

rows.value: The authors report that 2D power-law models produced a poor fit to downstream evaluations, which they attribute to noise and small dataset sizes compared with validation sets.
rows.note: The paper then fits a power law to the optima of the per-scale polynomial curves; this is not a test of generic held-out pretraining loss.
rows.check: This is a methods remark that the 2D Chinchilla form fit downstream NLL poorly, attributed to noise. It gives no fit statistics and no comparison of the resulting optima, so it shows no effect on exponents or split.

relationships.condition: Skill-specific optima vs Dubey et al. APE optimum, canonical datamix, 6e18–3e21 FLOPs
relationships.reason: The compute-optimal split depends on which loss is optimised. Knowledge QA optima sit above the APE parameter count, especially at low compute, while code optima sit below it (r1, r2). The validation-set choice shifts the optimum by more than 10% even at the largest scales (r10).
relationships.display_finding: Knowledge QA favored larger models than the APE optimum and code favored smaller ones, while validation-set choice shifted optimal size by more than 10% even at the largest scales.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Skill-specific optima vs Dubey et al. APE optimum, canonical datamix, 6e18–3e21 FLOPs
source_check.reason: Knowledge QA and code favour opposite allocation shifts from the APE reference (r1,r2); validation-set choice changes optimal parameter counts by over 30% at the smallest scale and over 10% at the largest three scales (r10). This qualifies transfer of an allocation across objectives.

relationships.condition: Skill, datamix and validation-set choices; datamix ablations only at 6e18 FLOPs
relationships.reason: Estimated optima move with the target skill (r1, r2), the skill-relevant data share (r3–r5), and the datamix and validation set (30–50% at 6e18; more than 10% at the largest scales) (r6, r7, r8, r10). Knowledge datamix results are noisier (r4).
relationships.display_finding: Estimated optima vary with target skill, relevant data share, mixture, and validation set, with reported shifts of 30–50% at 6×10^18 FLOPs and over 10% at the largest scales; mixture ablations cover only 6×10^18 FLOPs, and knowledge-mixture results are noisier.

source_check.reason: Optima depend on target skill (r1,r2) and validation set (r10). §§4.2–4.3 additionally demonstrate datamix-dependent optima at 6e18 FLOPs, with noisier knowledge-QA results.

relation.reason: The study trains IsoFLOP sweeps and directly compares loss-minimising allocations across skills, datamixes and validation sets.

tranche.reason: The study's experiments show that compute-optimal allocations require qualification by target skill, pretraining datamix and validation-set choice.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Skill-specific optima under the canonical datamix and tested data ablations
reader_labels.reason: Knowledge QA is more capacity-hungry than the APE optimum while code is more data-hungry; increasing skill-relevant data shifts both skills’ optima, and the shifts differ by skill (r1–r6). The study does not establish the claimed stable powers for both parameters and tokens.

reader_labels.reason: Optima and measured losses vary with skill-relevant data and validation-set composition, and the authors report a poor fit from the 2D power-law model on downstream evaluations (r3–r11).
